facts.text: Despite the name, the dusky woodswallow is not a true swallow; it belongs to the same family as butcherbirds, currawongs and the Australian magpie.
facts.quote: The name "woodswallow" is a misnomer as they are not closely related to true swallows. Instead, they belong to the family Artamidae, which also includes butcherbirds, currawongs and the Australian magpie.

facts.text: The dusky woodswallow has a black, white-tipped tail with a silver underwing and a blue-grey bill capped with black.
facts.quote: The dusky woodswallow has a black, white-tipped tail with a silver underwing. The birds have a blue-grey bill capped with black.

facts.text: A distinctive white patch on the outer wing sets the dusky woodswallow apart from other woodswallows.
facts.quote: In a significant difference from other woodswallows, dusky woodswallows have a distinctive white patch on the outer wing.

facts.text: They have been observed working as a group to rob a restless flycatcher of its prey, a behaviour called kleptoparasitism.
facts.quote: They have also been observed engaging in kleptoparasitism, working as a group to rob a restless flycatcher of its prey.

facts.text: The nest is a bowl of twigs and roots lined with grass, tucked behind bark or high in a tree branch, and built between August and January.
facts.quote: The nest of the dusky woodswallow consists of twigs, roots and other similar foliage matted together to form a bowl shape, which is lined with grass. It is positioned safely, behind bark, and/or high in a tree branch

facts.text: During the breeding season, dusky woodswallows nest in flocks of 20-30 birds to keep predators away from their young.
facts.quote: During the breeding season, they nest in large flocks to make sure to keep predators away from young. These flocks can be 20–30 dusky woodswallows in size.

facts.text: When a predator approaches, dusky woodswallows give a harsh mobbing call to warn the rest of the flock.
facts.quote: The most distinctive of these calls is perhaps the one which is used when a predator or intruder approaches, which consists of a harsh mobbing call to warn others.

facts.text: Dusky woodswallows eat termites, butterflies, other insects and even nectar from flowers.
facts.quote: Dusky woodswallows have been seen eating termites, butterflies and other insects. They also eat nectar from flowers.

facts.text: The female lays white eggs, usually no more than three or four.
facts.quote: The female lays white eggs, of which there are usually no more than three or four.

facts.text: Dusky woodswallows roost communally, usually at night.
